name: Quality healthcare critical towards reducing maternal deaths in Kenya

content.title: Quality healthcare critical towards reducing maternal deaths in Kenya
content.summary: The symposium, organized by Aga Khan University Medical College, East Africa and the University of San Francisco, California discussed interventions that exist to improve the quality of maternal healthcare for women in Kenya

content.text: Deaths of women and children in Kenya can easily be prevented if women receive quality healthcare during pregnancy and childbirth.

"Although great strides have been made in reducing maternal mortality, an estimated 6,300 Kenyan women, or one out of 270 pregnant women, die annually during childbirth, reflecting low utilization and quality of health services in the country," says Prof Marleen Temmerman, Director of the Centre of Excellence in Women and Child Health East Africa, Aga Khan University.

The symposium, organized by Aga Khan University Medical College, East Africa, the University of San Francisco, California and healthcare stakeholders discussed current research, solutions and interventions that exist to improve the quality of maternal healthcare services for women in Kenya.
Dr John Wekesa Masasabi, Director General, Ministry of Health said the Kenyan government has continuously prioritized the health of women, children and families.

"The government has made steady progress in improving reproductive, maternal and child outcomes. Child mortality has declined by over 20 per cent and the country achieved a total fertility rate of less than four. Antenatal coverage has increased to 96, and skilled care at childbirth has improved from 44% to 68%. In addition, over half of the women receive postnatal care within 48 hours of childbirth and the number of women at reproductive age using modern contraceptive has risen to more than 56%, " he said.

The Ministry of Health, through the National Maternal and Newborn Health Technical Working Group with support from WHO, has renewed its commitment towards reducing maternal and neonatal mortality in the country.
"We aim to scale up quality of care interventions that should lead to a reduction in facility-based deaths of mothers and neonates by half over the coming five years," added Dr Wekesa.

The high rates of maternal deaths in the country are attributed to preventable causes such as severe bleeding, obstructed labour, infections after childbirth, complication due to unsafe abortion, and high blood pressure.

Some of the recommendations to reduce maternal mortality include increased investment in health care, improvement of infrastructure for emergency obstetric and newborn care, increased investment in the rights and education of adolescent girls, and support in family planning services.

"Stakeholders in the health sector need to come together and step up efforts to address the health needs of women and girls in this country in order to achieve Goal 3 of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) agenda, which is to reduce the global maternal mortality ratio to fewer than 70 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births by 2030," added Prof Marleen.

The symposium was held as a build-up to the upcoming Nairobi Summit on International Conference on Population and Development (ICPD+25), a high-level conference to mobilize the political will and financial commitments to implement the ICPD Programme of Action.
